caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 57 of 2002 with (Civil Rule No. 156 (FM) of 2002).
lawyer:
Mohammad Ali Khan, Advocate------For the Appellants. 
Arun Kumar Battachira, Advocate------For the Respondents.
parties:
Ershad Ali (Md) and another ------ Appellants
Vs.
Rampada Das & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Purchaser (pre-emptee) presented the appeal against an order dated 11-12-2001 passed by the Subordinate Judge. Court No.2 at Jessore in Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 2000, which allowed pre-emption.

2. Respondent No. 1 on 2-9-97 made an application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 being Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1997 for pre-emption of transfer of the case land measuring about 2.89 acres of land appertaining to SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 fully described in the schedule to the application. The case was then renumbered as aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2000.

3. In the application, it is stated that SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 of mouje Helanchi under Thana Monirampur were recorded in the names of Eshan Chandra Das, Hazari Das, Rajbihari Das, Satish Chardra Das, Panchamoni Dasi and Sudhir Das in their specified shares. While jointly possessing his shares, Satish Chandra Das died leaving three sons, namely, the pre-emptor and respondent Nos. 2 and 3 (opposite party Nos. 4 and 5 in the application).

4. Besides, Panchamoni Dasi exhausted her interest in the holdings by transfer to the pre-emptor said respondent Nos.2 and 3 and Purnima Rani and Subola Rani Dasi and delivery of possession thereof.

5. Other co-sharer Hazari Das died leaving three sons namely, Durgapada, Kalipada Das and respondent No. 4 (Opposite party No.6 in the application). Kalipada Das already transferred his interest to the pre-emptor and Durga Das to said respondent No.4, Eshan Chandra Das died leaving his wife Hazu Rani Dasi as his only legal representative, Rajbihari Das also exhausted his interest in the' holdings by transfers to the pre-emptor and others. As per wish of Eshan Chandra Das on the death of Hazu Bala the pre-emptor and respondent Nos.2 and 3 inherited her share. Thus, the pre-emptor became co-sharer in the holdings both by inheritance as well as purchase.

6. Sudhir Kumar Das, opposite party No.3 in the application, by a registered deed being No.4715 dated 2-6-97 transferred the case land to the appellants at a consideration of Taka 3,00,000 without service of any notice upon the co-sharers and behind their back. On 13-8-97 obtaining certified copy of the impugned sale deed she became sure about the transfer and deposited in Court the consideration money along with statutory compensation for pre-emption of the case land.

7. Appellants opposed the application by filing a written objection. They admitted that said SA Khatian No. 589 and 596 were finally published recording the names of said Ehsan Chandra Das, Hazari Das, Rajbihari, Satish Chandra Das and Panchamoni Dasi and Sudhir Das to the extent of their respective shares.

8. Their further case is that Hazari, Rajbihari and Satish Das got the interest of Panchamani Dasi, After death of Satish Das his interest devolved upon Rampada Das (pre-emptor). Shyamapada and Joyanta, and after death of Hazari Lal Das his interest devolved upon his three sons, namely, Durgapada, Shibpada and Kalipada. After death of Eshan Das his share devolved upon his wife Hazubala. Hazubala transferred 1.8425 acres of land to Sudhir Kumar Das by a deed dated 30-6-80. Sudhir Kumar Das got his name mutated in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79- 80 and No.317/ IX-I/82-83 and possessed accordingly. As Sudhir Das possessed his entire land inherited and purchased under khatian No. 1102 and the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in such khatian the pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the impugned transfer.

9. They claimed that as the pre-emptor already disposed of all his land Including his share in the homestead and ceased to have any interest in the holdings; the application for pre-emption was therefore not maintainable.

10. Joyanta, brother of the pre-emptor along with the pre-emptor, mediated the sale by said opposite party No.3, Sudhir Kumar Das to the appellants. Price of the land was settled at Taka 5,00,000 and value of shallow machine, trees, etc. at Taka 1,50,000 and on 1-6-97 they paid Taka 6,50,000. As the pre-emptor assured them not to pre-empt the transfer, the price of the land was written in the deed at Taka 3,00,000 only.

11. On the pleadings following issues were settled: (a) Was the case maintainable in the manner and form as framed? (b) Was the case barred by limitation? (c) Was the case bad for defect of parties? (d) Was the case hit by principles of waiver and acquiescence? (e) Was the pre-emptor entitled to pre-empt the transfer dated 2-6-97 ? (f) What relief the pre-emptor was entitled to?

12. In support of his case, the pre-emptor examined three witnesses including himself. The appellant also examined three witnesses including himself. The appellants also examined three witnesses including appellant No.1, Copy of impugned sale deed dated 2-6-97 was marked as Exhibit-1 while the documents of the appellants were marked as Exhibit 'Ka' to 'Cha'.

13. Upon the evidence oral and documentary on record learned Subordinate Judge found that the. pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the holding while the appellants strangers; the application for pre-emption was not barred by limitation and not bad for defect of parties; the appellants failed to prove their case that the right of pre-emption was barred by principles of waiver and acquiescence and the order dated 16-10-79 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79-80 opening new Khatian No. 1102 was not valid for want of service of notice upon Satish Chandra Das (father of the pre-emptor) and order dated 17-2-83 passed in 317/IX-I/82-83 did not, in fact, open any khatian, and would not be binding upon the pre-emptor.

14. Upon such findings, learned Subordinate Judge allowed the application for pre-emption by impugned judgment and order.

15. Mr Mohammad Ali Khan, learned Advocate for the appellants, challenged the order on various grounds.

16. Firstly, he submitted that in view of said orders passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX- I/79-80 and 317/IX-I/82-83 opening new khatians in the name of Sudhir Kumar Das in respect of his entire land and payment of rents on the basis of such khatian the pre-emptor was not entitled to pre-empt the impugned transfer since he was not a co-sharer in any of such holdings.

17. In support he cited case of Md Jabed All and others vs Rakhal Chandra Mandal and others 33 DLR (AD) 309; Abdur Rouf vs Ahmuda Khatun. 33 DLR (AD) 323; Md Rais Ali vs Imam Hossain and others. 33 DIR 318; Chandra Kumar vs Abdul Motaleb 19 DLR (SC) 36 and Md Khairullah Bhuiyan vs Haji Nurul Alam, 35 DLR (AD) 338.

18. In the written objection, it is stated that Sudhir Kumar Das possessed his shares by separa- tion and amalgamation in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-I/79-80 and under new Khatian No. 1102. Then, after purchase of 1.8425 acres of land from Hazubala he got his name again separated and amalgamated in Miscellaneous Case being No. 317/IX-I/82-83. Consequently, the pre-emptor who was not a co-sharer in such separated and amalgamated holdings was not entitled to pre-empt.

19. Appellant No.1 as OPW-1 deposed in support of such case. He said that appellant No.2 was his younger brother. Hazubala transferred 1.8425 acres to Sudhir Kumar Das. Sudhir Das got that land mutated in his name in Miscellaneous Case No. 317/IX-I/82-83. Sudhir Das also got his name mutated in Miscellaneous Case No.45/IX-I/79-S0. The pre-emptor was not a co-sharer in such mutated holdings. He did not see as to whether those mutated Khatians were mentioned in the impugned sale deed. He however denied that Sudhir Das did not file Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX.-1/79-80 and obtained an antedated order therein.

20. Orders passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-1/79-80 and No. 317/IX-I/82-S3 were adduced as Exhibit 'Ka' and 'Ka-1'. Four rent receipts were also adduced as Exhibit 'Gha' to 'Gha-3'. Of them, Exhibit 'Gha-2' and 'Gha-3' show payment of rents under impugned khatian No.1102. None of the rent receipts was proved by any witness. Even OPW-1 Ershad Ali in his deposition did not claim that Sudhir Das or anybody else ever paid rents under such Khatians No.1102 or 1134.

21. By ex parte order dated 16-10-79, Exhibit- 'Ka' the Circle Officer (Rev) at Manirampur allowed separation and amalgamation of said SA Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 and opened new Khatian No. 1102 in respect of 2.46 acres of land in the name of Sudhir Kumar Das. By another ex parte order dated 17-2-83 Exhibit-'Ka-1' the Circle Officer (Rev) purportedly again allowed separation and amalgamation of 1.8425 acre of land in the name of said Sudhir Kumar Das. But, in the orders space meant for writing Khatian No. and amount of rent is found vacant. No other evidence is found on record to prove that said Khatian No. 1134 was at all opened by said Circle Officer.

22. OPW 2 brought the record of said miscellaneous cases. After perusal of the record of mutation proceedings the learned Subordinate Judge found that return of the notice does not show that Satish Chandra Das, father of the pre-emptor, received the notice and/or anybody else received the notice on his behalf. We have also examined the undated return of the notice of Miscellaneous Case No. 45/IX-1/79-80 by one Md Mojam Ali, peon Exhibit-'Uma (Uma)' and find that the notice was not at all served upon Satish Chandra Das, father of the pre-emptor. We could not find any notice of other mutation case in the record. Sudhir Kumar Das has not been examined. Nor any explanation was furnished for his non-examination.

23. OPW 3 Santosh Kumar Das proved the agreement which is marked as Exhibit 'Gha' and 'Cha(1)' for sale of shallow machine, trees, etc.

<u>24. It is now well settled by good authorities including those cited above that the pre-emptor must not only have a subsisting interest in the holding when he makes the application for pre-emption. but must continue to hold such interest until disposal of such proceeding for pre-emption. And a co-sharer means a person whose interest subsists throughout the course of the proceedings for pre-emption and not a person who had such interest in the holding at the time of making the application but lost it before disposal of the case. A fresh interest acquired at a later stage cannot be tacked on the interest held at the commencement of the proceeding but lost during the proceeding; Cf: Chandra Kumar vs Abdul Motaleb, 19 DLR (SC) 36 and Mofizuddin Patwari vs Abdul Hakim and others, 33 DLR (AD) 305.</u>

<u>25. Secondly, if the record of rights is changed by way of mutation in accordance with the procedure laid down in law by a valid order before the commencement of the -proceeding for pre-emption the pre-emptor must be held to cease to have any interest in the holding. When such mutation was ordered after service of notice upon the pre-emptor such order would be binding upon him. But if mutation brought about without any service of notice upon the pre-emptor, such sub-division of the holding would not be binding upon the pre-emptor. In Md Jabed Ali and others vs Rakhal Chandra Mandai and others 33 DLR (AD) 309, the Appellate Division held that-</u>

" ...when ,an order is passed, by competent Revenue Officer under section 117 (of the State, Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950) and the order is in conformity with the statutory requirements and the order has been given effect by the co-sharer tenants of the holding the holding stands separated under the law"

26. So, in order to bind and/or disentitle the pre-emptor to pre-empt, the order separating and/ or subdividing the existing holding must be shown to have been passed by a competent authority after compliance with the law namely, after due service of notice upon all co-sharer tenants of the holding and such separation must be given effect to or acted upon by such tenants.

27. It is also needless to say, in deciding an application for pre-emption limited jurisdiction of the Court is now well recognised to examine as to whether or not subdivision of the existing holding in question is valid.

28. In the case ,before us we find there was an order passed by the revenue authority for opening a new khatian being No. 1102 in respect of 2.46 acres of land ata jama of Taka 4.30. As found already, the order was passed without any service of notice upon Satish Chandra Das, father of the pre-emptor. Moreover, no evidence could be adduced that such order and/or subdivision of the holdings was acted upon by the co-sharer tenants of the holdings. Payment of rents on the basis of such mutation Khatian by the co-sharer tenants over a period of seventeen year; could not be proved.

<u>29. Last but not the least, vendor Sudhir Kumar Das transferred the land of Khatian Nos. 589 and 596 and the appellants purchased the same land of said holdings. Mere reading of the deed clearly evidences the intention of the appellants to purchase land of impugned khatians not new Khatian No. 1102. Now, sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act would not permit them to introduce any other intention of the parties to disentitle pre-emption.</u>

30. Mr Mohammad All Khan submitted that in case of pre-emption unless necessity for pre- emption could be proved the pre-emptor would not be entitled to pre-emption. In support, he relied upon aforesaid Ahmed Hossain and others vs Basharat Hossain and others 32 DLR (AD) 54.

31. In the application for pre-emption, the pre- emptor averred that he was a co-sharer by inheritance and purchase in the holdings. Transferred .land was a part of their ancestral homestead. He was living with his family therein. They needed the land for maintenance of privacy and dignity. In evidence, the pre-emptor as PW 1 testified in support of such averments. Such case of pre-emptor on necessity was never dented by the appellants. Intention of the pre-emptor therefore, cannot be termed as luxury, Moreover, the purchaser appellants belonged to separate community from that of the pre-emptor. If they are allowed to enter into the homestead very object and purpose of the law for pre-emption would be frustrated.

32. Lastly, he submitted that the pre-emptor already disposed of all his land acquired by inheritance and purchase. He also drew our attention to the documents filed in Court. Learned Subordinate Judge considered the question and found that the appellants hopelessly failed to prove that the pre-emptor disposed of all his interest in the suit holdings by way of transfer and thereby, ceased to have any right to pre-empt.

33. Mr Mohammad Ali Khan also submitted that the pre-emptor himself filed documents by which he purchased 1.745 acres of land. The appellants also filed copy of documents by which the pre-emptor already disposed of all his shares by transfer. No attempt was however taken by them to prove any of the documents, none of documents was tendered and marked Exhibit. Accordingly, trial Court had to exclude them from consideration, After examination of tile record, we also could not find any substance in such submissions that the pre-emptor ceased to have the right to pre-empt.

34. Attempt of the appellants to disentitle the pre-emptor from pre-empting the transfer on the principles of waiver and/or acquiescence is so ridiculous that the trial Court rightly rejected such plea.

35. No other issue was taken on behalf of the appellants.

36. In above view of the matter, we find the impugned judgment and order of the trial Court do not suffer from any illegality or infirmity, Appeal accordingly, fails.

37. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with cost. Impugned judgment and order allowing pre-emption are hereby affirmed. In view of order of dismissal of the appeal, connected Civil Rule No. 156 (FM) of 2002 is also discharged with cost, Order of stay granted at the time of issue of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the records at once.

End.
